_comment: The property tax increase, tracked per fiscal year. Every figure here is transcribed from a source meeting; `evidence` names where. Rates are decimal multipliers applied to taxable value, matching the Truth-in-Taxation schedule read into the record. `rates.adopted` is what the council actually set on August 6 and what the page is about; `rates.proposed` is the 0.001700 it noticed and did not adopt, kept because the notice, the schedule and every figure quoted before that night were built on it.
purpose: Public safety — the Utah County Sheriff's Office Eagle Mountain Division, including deputies added to keep pace with the city's growth.
residential_ratio_note: Utah taxes a primary residence on 55% of market value. Business, rental, and secondary property is taxed on the full value.

certified_2026.label: 2026 certified rate
certified_2026.derivation: The city never published this as a rate; it is implied by its own Truth-in-Taxation notice, and the notice's two published figures imply it slightly differently. A $314.03 rise on a $488,000 primary residence against the 0.001700 proposal implies 0.00053014; the noticed 220.9% implies 0.00052976. Both round to 0.000530, which is the rate stated here — but 0.001700 against 0.000530 is +220.75%, so the noticed 220.9% cannot be reproduced to the decimal from any single rounded rate. The gap is a tenth of a point and lives inside a certified rate the city has never published. Utah County delivered the recalculated certified rate on June 22, after the June 16 schedule was read.

adopted.label: Adopted 2026–27
adopted.note: Public safety · +183.02% over the certified rate
adopted.pct_basis: Increase over the 2026 certified rate of 0.000530 — the same basis the notice used, and the figure stated in the motion. It measures the rate, not collections, and not anyone's total bill.
adopted.vote: Passed 5–0 on a roll call — moved by Whiting, seconded by Wright; Wood, Whiting, Wright, Clark and Huish all in favour
adopted.motion: Approves and adopts a property tax rate of 0.001500 for fiscal year 2026 to 2027. This rate exceeds the certified tax rate of 0.000530 and will result in an increase in the city's ad valorem property tax budgeted revenue of approximately $5,591,594, or 183.02% above the city's property tax budgeted revenue for the prior year, exclusive of new growth.

home_example.note: The Truth-in-Taxation notice's own average home. Its $268,400 taxable value — 55% of $488,000 — times the 0.000970 the rate rose over the certified rate. The notice put the same home at $314.03 under the 0.001700 that was noticed. Around the table the council called it “about $250 a year” and “closer to 70 cents per day”; those are this figure spoken loosely, not a different one.

adopted.derivation: The rate, the 183.02% and the $5,591,594 are read verbatim from the motion Councilmember Whiting made and the council passed 5–0 on August 6; nothing about them is inferred. The $8,646,795 is the one derived figure: the noticed schedule's $9,798,139 less the $1,151,344 the council took off the increase ($6,742,938 noticed against $5,591,594 adopted). It prices out against the same citywide taxable value the 0.001700 schedule implies to within 0.02%, which is the check that it is the right kind of number.

proposed.label: Noticed 2026–27, not adopted
proposed.note: Superseded by the adopted 0.001500 · was +220.9% over the certified rate
proposed.pct_basis: Increase over the 2026 certified rate of 0.000530. This is the figure in the city's Truth-in-Taxation notice, and it measures the rate, not collections.
proposed.derivation: Confirmed twice over by the schedule read on June 16: a $500,000 primary residence at $467.43 in total city tax, and an average business at $4,341.62 on a $2,554,303 market value, each independently imply a rate of 0.0016997 — 0.001700 at the six decimal places the city publishes. The same rate reconciles with the 2026 Truth-in-Taxation notice. It is not the rate in force: on August 6 the council adopted 0.001500 instead.

tentative.label: Tentative schedule, read May 26
tentative.derivation: Implied by the schedule read into the record on May 26: 0.000534 × (9,798,139 ÷ 2,839,998). Reproduces that schedule's own examples exactly — a $500,000 primary residence at $146.85 now and $506.64 proposed, an increase of $359.79. The certified rate has since been recalculated and the proposal set at 0.001700.

revenue_increase_note: The noticed schedule's own figure: $9,798,139 against the $2,839,998 the city collects today. The adopted rate's equivalent is $5,806,797, and the motion's own $5,591,594 — the figure the council voted on — is measured against prior-year budgeted revenue exclusive of new growth instead. See `rates.adopted`.
revenue_ratio_note: Collections against collections: $2,839,998 today against the $8,646,795 the adopted rate raises is a 204.5% increase. That is a larger number than the 183.02% in the motion, because the motion compares rates against the certified rate rather than comparing collections. The noticed 0.001700 would have been 245%.

as_read.note: On June 16 the mayor read the increase as 218%. That is 0.001700 measured against 0.000534, the rate then in effect — the county had not yet returned the recalculated certified rate, which he noted was due on June 22. Against that recalculated 0.000530 the same proposal is the 220.9% now noticed.
as_read.examples_note: The worked examples the mayor read aloud on June 16, transcribed from the recording. They are cents off what 0.001700 gives exactly, because the city computed them from the unrounded rate before rounding it to six decimals for publication.

source.quote_note: Read as item 17.B. The mayor prefaced it: the schedule was current as of June 11, because Utah County would not return the actual certified figure until June 22.

meetings.title: Council declares intent to raise property tax
meetings.note: Three resolutions in one night: accepted the FY2026–27 tentative budget, acknowledged the Budget Officer's statement of a proposed increase, and declared intent to raise revenue above the certified rate. Mayor Gray read the impact schedule here for the first time; the minutes record that he read it but do not reprint the figures. Both August hearings were set at this meeting.

Declaring intent to increase property tax revenue, providing notice, and setting the Truth-in-Taxation hearing for August 6, 2026 at 6:00 PM

meetings.title: Mayor reads the tentative tax impact schedule
meetings.note: The required Truth-in-Taxation impact schedule was read aloud: a 245% increase in city property tax revenue, earmarked for the Sheriff's contract. Council then reviewed the tentative budget. No votes taken. These figures implied a rate of 0.001842 and were superseded on June 16.

meetings.title: Schedule read a third time; budget manager presents the tentative budget
meetings.note: Taken up under a heading marked “no action taken.” The minutes record that Mayor Gray read the Property Tax Impact Schedule but do not reprint its figures, so it is not possible to say from the record whether this was the 245% schedule or an early version of the revised one. The recording does not settle it either: it runs 2h 39m and ends partway through public comment, before item 18 was reached.

FY2026–27 budget discussion; Budget Manager Terrence Dela Pena presented the proposed tentative budget

meetings.title: Council adopts the interim budget and the proposed certified tax rate
meetings.note: The night the real number reached the record. Mayor Gray read the Proposed Tax Impact Schedule — the 0.001700 the city went on to notice — and Council then took public comment and adopted it, 4–1. That was the rate proposed; on August 6 the council set 0.001500 instead. Minutes approved July 7, 2026. The minutes note that the schedule was read but do not reprint its figures; those are transcribed from the recording.

items.text: Proposed Tax Impact Schedule read into the record (information only)
Resolution adopting the FY2026–27 interim budget and the proposed certified tax rate; discontinuing DebtBook services

meetings.title: Residents take opposite sides; council spends half an hour on it
meetings.note: Nothing about the tax was on the agenda, and it still took up more of the night than most items that were. Bronwyn Richardson opposed what she called a 220% increase, citing the two Title I elementary schools and the Title I preschool in the city, and asked for a line-by-line accounting given that the notice says the money is entirely for public safety while officials had also described it as employee compensation. Jeff Ruth, of The Landing, took the other side at the end of a comment about parking: “If it's all going towards law enforcement and fire, I fully support it… from somebody that struggles month to month, there's been many times I've called officers out and I never saw them.” In council comments afterward, Councilmember Rich Wood corrected a common reading of the proposal — “there's not extra money… it's all going to pay for our entire contract, not new… our entire contract with the Sheriff's Department” — and apologized for how the city had explained it. The June 16 minutes were approved this night, inside the consent agenda as item 14.A.

items.text: Public comment — two residents on the proposed increase, one against and one for
Minutes of the June 16, 2026 meeting, approved within the consent agenda

meetings.title: Council ties the increase to the deputies it would pay for
meetings.note: Not on the agenda and not discussed as an item. During closing council comments on a neighborhood's speeding complaint, Councilmember Craig Whiting named it in passing — “the tax increase is going to be discussed here soon and voted on” — and said the deputies it would fund were what he expected to bring more patrol into neighborhoods. Listed so the record between the June 16 vote and the August hearing has no silent gap in it.

meetings.title: Council adopts 0.001500, not the 0.001700 it noticed
meetings.note: The statutory hearing on the increase itself, set by resolution 17.C. on May 5, and the night the rate was actually set. Roughly sixty people spoke over nearly three hours, almost all of them against the advertised 220%; the hearing closed at 9:00 PM and the council then talked the rate down and adopted 0.001500 — 183.02% over the 0.000530 certified rate, raising $5,591,594 rather than the $6,742,938 on the notice. Councilmember Huish opened the responses with an apology on how the increase had been explained — "we failed you" — and said the "100% public safety" framing came from the application filed with the state, which was built around covering the Sheriff's contract entirely with property tax. Council also agreed to bring back an ordinance requiring an annual rate review, and a resolution creating a dedicated public safety fund. Minutes not yet published; the figures here are transcribed from the recording, and every rate on this page is the adopted 0.001500 except where it says otherwise.

meetings.title: Budget adoption hearing
meetings.note: Where the FY2026–27 budget is finally adopted. Set by resolution 17.A. on May 5. What passed on June 16 was an interim budget; this is the final one. Public comment is taken.

meetings.title: Sheriff's Office presents deputy options
meetings.note: Chief Deputy Sheriff Erik Knutzen laid out staffing options, including additional deputies — the spending the increase is meant to fund. The increase itself was not named.

meetings.title: Council works through revenue generation
meetings.note: Two-day strategic and budget retreat in St. George covering revenue generation and the budget. The increase itself was not named in the minutes.

meetings.title: Capital projects walkthrough
meetings.note: Staff walked Council through the water, wastewater, and stormwater projects in the proposed budget. Other taxes come up as funding sources — the RAP tax, the transient room tax, sales-tax exactions — but the full transcript never once mentions property tax.

record.label: On the record
record.note: Meetings where the increase was acted on, read into the record, or taken up in front of the public. The schedule has been read four times.

hearing.label: The two hearings
hearing.note: The Truth-in-Taxation hearing on August 6 set the rate at 0.001500. The budget-adoption hearing on August 18 is still to come, and the increase does not take effect until the full budget passes there.
